title: Adab with the earth
hookLine: the end of the world arrives, and there's a seedling in your hand

cards: The Hour has come. The end of everything. And there you are, holding a small palm shoot, roots still in a clump of soil.
What now? The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, answered that exact question.
In the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, in paraphrase: if the Hour is established and one of you has a seedling in his hand, and he is able to plant it before he stands up, let him plant it.

teach.h: PLANT IT, EVEN AT THE END.
teach.b: Sit with how strange that is. If the world is ending, nobody will eat the dates or rest in the shade. And still: plant it.
The hadith pulls the act loose from its result. Then the Qur'an gives the reason the earth is in our hands at all.
Surah al-Baqarah, in Pickthall's translation: "Lo! I am about to place a viceroy in the earth." Khalifa: a deputy, a steward, someone looking after what belongs to another.
In Sahih Muslim, in paraphrase, the Prophet adds: the world is sweet and green, and Allah has made you successors in it, to see how you act. Stewards are watched for how they treat the estate.
Then a hadith that turns the garden into worship.
In Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase: whenever a Muslim plants a tree or sows a crop, and a bird, or a person, or an animal eats from it, it counts as charity for him.
By that hadith, even the sparrow that steals your figs leaves a charity behind. So the adab with the earth comes down to three movements. Plant, even when you won't see the fruit.
Look after it as a steward, not an owner. And let the birds have their share. That closes the manners of daily life, down to the soil underfoot.
Tomorrow the path turns inward, to the virtues.

how: Islamic teaching on the earth draws on the Qur'an's description of humanity as khalifa, a steward on the earth, and on hadith that count planting as charity and that urge planting a seedling even when the Hour comes.

games.q: what does “adab with the earth” mean?
o: the rules for buying and selling land fairly in the market
the belief that the earth is holy and must never be farmed
a steward's manners: plant, look after it, and share the harvest

games.q: adab with the earth — tap the pairs.

s: the hadith says plant only if you'll live to see the fruit
plant it even when the Hour has come and no one will eat from it.
what a bird eats from your crop counts as charity
a bird, a person or an animal eats from it, and it is charity (Bukhari).
al-Baqarah describes a viceroy placed in the earth
Pickthall: Lo! I am about to place a viceroy in the earth.

games.q: the Hour has come. you are holding a seedling and have time to put it in the ground. what does the hadith say?
games.why: if he is able to plant it before he stands up, let him plant it (Musnad Ahmad).

practice: Feel your weight resting on the ground, or on a floor built on the ground, and bring to mind one small patch of earth you can reach: a pot on the windowsill, a yard, a crack in the sidewalk where something is already trying.

Picture putting something into it, a seed, a cutting, or water for a thirsty plant, and notice you don't need to see it grow. If you pray, you can offer that small planting with the remembrance of Allah.

wordCard.voice: Adab with the earth. The manners of a steward: planting even when you won't see the fruit, looking after what was entrusted, and letting the birds have their share. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a seedling or young palm shoot, the word in the hadith.

carryVoice: Your line: plant it anyway. The birds get their share too. Rest well.

sources.ref: Musnad Ahmad (Anas ibn Malik: if the Hour comes and one of you holds a seedling, let him plant it); also in al-Bukhari's al-Adab al-Mufrad
